# ASTC differential fixtures

`astc-<variant>-<N>x<N>.bin` are ASTC payloads produced by ARM's `astcenc`
through the `astc-encoder-py` binding, at each of Unity's six block footprints
in four variants: opaque LDR, LDR with a diagonal alpha ramp, an HDR gradient,
and `hdr-glow`, an HDR image made for the HDR paths the smooth gradient does
not reach (below). Each covers a surface two blocks wide and two blocks tall,
so the comparison sees block-to-block placement and not just one block's
decode. The source images are computed by `tools/generate_astc_fixtures.py`,
which regenerates these files; the formulas live in the script rather than in
committed PNGs.

ASTC was the last block format outside the managed differential, and the reason
was that the other formats there are fed pseudorandom bytes. That works for
them because every bit pattern decodes to something. ASTC is not like that:
random data lands on reserved block encodings no encoder emits, and the two
implementations part ways on those by design -- the managed decoder substitutes
an error colour where this crate rejects the block -- so a random-payload
comparison would report a disagreement that says nothing about either decoder.
Real encoder output contains no reserved blocks, which is what makes the
comparison mean something.

## The astcenc reference blobs

`astc-<variant>-<N>x<N>-astcenc.rgba` hold what Khronos `astcenc` 5.7.0
decompresses all twenty-four payloads to, regenerated by
`tools/decode_astc_references.py` from the committed payloads and an `astcenc`
binary. They are the normative reference for ASTC decoding: the
specification's own codec, decoding to the bytes GPUs and every conformant
decoder produce, independent of the AssetStudio decoder lineage this crate was
ported from. LDR payloads are decoded with `-dl` to eight bits. HDR payloads
are decoded with `-dH` to half floats, and each channel is clamped to [0, 1]
and rounded to eight bits, which is the conversion this crate applies to a
decoded HDR value.

The lineage matters because that lineage disagrees with the specification by
one. The specification's `unorm16` decode keeps the top byte of the
interpolated 16-bit value; AssetStudio's decoders -- managed, C++, and the
`texture2ddecoder` port -- round a `* 255 / 65535` rescale instead, which
differs by one on some values. This crate used to inherit that, and its
output differed from `astcenc` on 2.7% to 27% of bytes depending on the
footprint, always by exactly one. It now follows the specification.

`ldr_astc_decodes_exactly_like_the_khronos_reference` in `texture.rs` pins
this crate's LDR output against these blobs byte for byte, and the managed
differential re-earns them against the crate's live output on every run.

`hdr_astc_decodes_exactly_like_the_khronos_reference` does the same for both
HDR variants. The `hdr` gradient decodes identically under every revision of
this decoder, so on its own it pins little; `hdr-glow` exists for two paths it
misses. Its fade changes hue as well as level, so the HDR RGB endpoint modes
carry negative deltas, which an earlier revision sign-extended into large
positive values and decoded with channels up to 255 levels off. Its top-left
block is one flat colour, which the encoder stores as an HDR void-extent
block, with half floats that scale to 255ths with a fraction above one half:
truncating them instead of rounding puts every channel of that block one level
low. The `hdr` references equal the managed blobs below byte for byte.

## The managed blobs

`astc-<variant>-<N>x<N>-managed.rgba` hold what the managed decoder produces.
They play two different roles.

For the six HDR formats they record exact agreement. `texture2ddecoder` 0.1.2
ported the reference `f32_to_u8` with `floor` where the C++ has `roundf`; the
first-party fork in `astc.rs` restored that word, and
`hdr_astc_decodes_exactly_like_the_managed_decoder` in `texture.rs` checks the
crate against these blobs byte by byte. The `hdr-glow` payloads have no
managed blob and are not part of the managed differential.

For the twelve LDR formats they record a declared divergence: the managed
decoder's rounded rescale against this crate's specification conversion.
`ldr_astc_differs_from_the_managed_decoder_only_by_rounding` in `texture.rs`
asserts the divergence is real and never exceeds one per byte, so a
divergence of any other shape or size fails -- and so does the managed
decoder silently converging, which is the signal to retire the declared
divergence and move LDR back into the exact set.

The managed differential checks every blob against the live managed decoder
on each run, so calling them managed output stays earned rather than
remembered.
